name: Show how a single formal neuron with the unit step activation (σ(ξ) = 1 for ξ ≥ 0, else 0) computes AND, OR and NOT. Give the weights and justify them.
answer:
All neurons have the formal input x0 = 1 with bias w0 and inner potential ξ = w0 + Σ wixi; inputs are from {0, 1}.

AND(x1, …, xn): bias w0 = −n, all weights wi = 1. Then ξ = −n + Σ xi, which is ≥ 0 iff all n inputs are 1.

OR(x1, …, xn): bias w0 = −1, all weights wi = 1. Then ξ = −1 + Σ xi ≥ 0 iff at least one input is 1.

NOT(x1): bias w0 = 0, weight w1 = −1. Then ξ = −x1, which is ≥ 0 (output 1) iff x1 = 0, and negative (output 0) for x1 = 1.

Geometrically each of these neurons is a hyperplane cutting off the appropriate corner(s) of the Boolean cube {0,1}n.
keyPoints: AND: bias −n, weights 1 → ξ = −n + Σ x_i ≥ 0 iff all inputs are 1
OR: bias −1, weights 1 → ξ ≥ 0 iff some input is 1
NOT: bias 0, weight −1 → ξ = −x_1 ≥ 0 iff x_1 = 0
Unit step outputs 1 exactly when ξ ≥ 0

name: State and prove the theorem about two-layer MLPs and Boolean functions.
answer:
Theorem. Let σ be the unit step function. Two-layer MLPs (i.e. with one hidden layer), where each neuron has σ as the activation function, are able to compute all functions of the form F : {0,1}n → {0,1}.

Proof.
Step 1 – a neuron recognising one vector. Given a vector v = (v1, …, vn) ∈ {0,1}n, consider a neuron Nv with
• bias w0 = −Σi=1..n vi,
• weights wi = 1 if vi = 1 and wi = −1 if vi = 0.
The output of Nv is 1 iff the input is v. Verification: for input x, ξ = −Σ vi + Σi: vi=1 xi − Σi: vi=0 xi. For x = v we get ξ = −Σ vi + Σ vi − 0 = 0 ≥ 0, so the output is 1. For x ≠ v, either some position with vi = 1 has xi = 0 (the positive sum loses at least 1) or some position with vi = 0 has xi = 1 (at least 1 is subtracted), so ξ ≤ −1 < 0 and the output is 0.

Step 2 – combine. The hidden layer consists of all neurons Nv for the vectors v satisfying F(v) = 1. Connect the outputs of all these neurons using an output neuron implementing OR (bias −1, weights 1).

Correctness. For an input x, at most the neuron Nx fires, and it is present in the hidden layer iff F(x) = 1. Hence the OR neuron outputs 1 iff F(x) = 1, i.e. the network computes F. □

(The verification inequalities in Step 1 spell out the slide's claim "output is 1 iff the input is v". Note that the construction may need up to 2n hidden neurons.)
keyPoints: Theorem: two-layer unit-step MLPs compute every F : {0,1}^n → {0,1}
Neuron N_v: bias −Σ v_i, weight 1 where v_i = 1 and −1 where v_i = 0
N_v outputs 1 iff the input equals v (ξ = 0 for x = v, ξ ≤ −1 otherwise)
Hidden layer: one neuron N_v for every v with F(v) = 1
Output neuron implements OR of the hidden neurons
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slide 43 (OR neuron from slide 42)

name: Explain non-linear separation by three-layer networks with unit step activations: what does each layer do geometrically, and how can such networks "approximate" any "reasonable" subset of the input space?
answer:
Consider a three-layer network in which each neuron has the unit step activation. The network divides the input space into two subspaces according to the output (0 or 1).

Role of the layers:
• The first (hidden) layer divides the input space into half-spaces (each neuron = one separating hyperplane).
• The second layer may e.g. make intersections of the half-spaces ⇒ convex sets (a neuron implementing AND).
• The third layer may e.g. make unions of some convex sets (a neuron implementing OR).

Approximating any reasonable set A ⊆ ℝk:
1. Cover A with hypercubes (squares in 2D, cubes in 3D, …).
2. Each hypercube K can be separated using a two-layer network NK, i.e. the function computed by NK gives 1 for points in K and 0 for the rest (a hypercube is an intersection of half-spaces: first-layer neurons give its faces, a second-layer neuron their intersection).
3. Finally, connect the outputs of the nets NK satisfying K ∩ A ≠ ∅ using a neuron implementing OR.

The resulting three-layer network outputs 1 exactly on the union of the selected hypercubes, which approximates A the better the finer the cover is.
keyPoints: First layer: half-spaces
Second layer: intersections of half-spaces → convex sets
Third layer: unions of convex sets
Cover A with hypercubes; each hypercube K separated by a two-layer net N_K
OR over the nets N_K with K ∩ A ≠ ∅

name: What does the lecture claim about the power of two-layer ReLU networks with one input, and what is the basic idea behind the claims (how a sum of simple ReLU-built functions produces the target function)?
answer:
Network type: a two-layer network with a single input and a single output; hidden neurons with the ReLU activation σ(ξ) = max(ξ, 0); the output neuron with the identity activation σ(ξ) = ξ (a linear model).

Claim 1 (function approximation): for every continuous function f : [0,1] → [0,1] and every ε > 0 there is a network of the above type computing a function F : [0,1] → ℝ such that |f(x) − F(x)| ≤ ε for all x ∈ [0,1].

Claim 2 (classification): for every open subset A ⊆ [0,1] there is a network of the above type such that for "most" x ∈ [0,1] we have x ∈ A iff the network's output is > 1/2 for the input x.

Basic idea of Claim 1 (picture): the network computes a weighted sum of ReLUs, which is a piecewise linear function. In the picture, several black "tent" (triangle) functions are drawn next to each other and the red curve is their sum – "Red = sum of black". Each tent is itself a combination of a few shifted ReLUs, so the output neuron can sum tents of suitable heights to obtain a piecewise linear function that follows f within ε (a continuous function on [0,1] can be approximated arbitrarily well by a piecewise linear one if the pieces are short enough).

Idea of Claim 2: reduce it to Claim 1. Take g(x) = min{1, dist(x, [0,1] ∖ A)/δ}: g is continuous, g = 0 outside A, and g < 1 only on a part of A whose measure → 0 as δ → 0. Approximate g within 1/4 by a network; then the output is > 1/2 where g = 1 and < 1/2 outside A, so only the small part of A where g < 1 may be misclassified.
keyPoints: Two-layer net, one input, ReLU hidden neurons, identity (linear) output
Any continuous f : [0,1] → [0,1] approximated within ε on all of [0,1]
Any open A ⊆ [0,1] recognised for "most" x by output > 1/2
Idea: sum of ReLU-built tent functions = piecewise linear approximation
Classification via g(x) = min{1, dist(x, [0,1]∖A)/δ} approximated within 1/4
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slides 46–47 (slide 47 is a figure; the tent/ReLU explanation interprets it)

name: State Cybenko's theorem in both versions presented (non-linear separation and function approximation), explain the terms "sigmoidal", "reasonable" and "most", and mention the later generalisations noted on the slide.
answer:
A continuous function σ is sigmoidal if σ(x) → 1 for x → +∞ and σ(x) → 0 for x → −∞.

Theorem (Cybenko 1989 – informal classification version). Let σ be a continuous sigmoidal function. For every "reasonable" set A ⊆ [0,1]n there is a two-layer network, where each hidden neuron has the activation function σ (output neurons are linear), such that for "most" vectors v ∈ [0,1]n we have: v ∈ A iff the network output is > 0 for the input v.
For the mathematically oriented: "reasonable" means Lebesgue measurable; "most" means that the set of incorrectly classified vectors has Lebesgue measure smaller than a given ε > 0.

Theorem (Cybenko 1989 – function approximation). Let σ be a continuous sigmoidal function. For every continuous function f : [0,1]n → [0,1] and every ε > 0 there is a function F : [0,1]n → ℝ computed by a two-layer network, where each hidden neuron has the activation function σ (output neurons are linear), such that |f(v) − F(v)| < ε for every v ∈ [0,1]n.

Generalisations: independently shown by Hornik, Stinchcombe & White (1989). The same holds for every continuous activation function that is not a polynomial – including ReLU (Leshno, Lin, Pinkus & Schocken 1993).
keyPoints: Sigmoidal: continuous, tends to 1 at +∞ and to 0 at −∞
Two-layer network, hidden activation σ, linear output neurons
Classification: v ∈ A iff output > 0 for "most" v (error set of measure < ε)
"Reasonable" = Lebesgue measurable
Approximation: |f(v) − F(v)| < ε for every v ∈ [0,1]^n, f continuous
Holds for every continuous non-polynomial activation, including ReLU

name: The universal approximation theorems concern two-layer networks. What is known today "beyond two layers" – about size, depth, width, transformers and the relation between expressivity and learnability?
answer:
• Size: the theorems say nothing about size – the hidden layer may need to be astronomically large.
• Depth helps: there are functions computable by small deep networks that any shallow network can approximate only with exponentially many neurons (Telgarsky 2016; Eldan & Shamir 2016).
• Width is not everything: deep ReLU networks with only n + 1 neurons per layer are universal approximators of continuous functions on [0,1]n (Hanin & Sellke 2017).
• Transformers (later in the course) approximate any continuous sequence-to-sequence function (Yun et al. 2020; Merrill & Sabharwal 2023, 2024).
• Expressivity ≠ learnability: whether gradient descent actually finds such weights is a different question.
keyPoints: The theorems give no bound on size – the hidden layer may be astronomically large
Depth helps: small deep nets vs. exponentially large shallow nets
Deep ReLU nets of width n + 1 are universal approximators on [0,1]^n
Transformers approximate continuous sequence-to-sequence functions
Expressivity ≠ learnability (gradient descent may not find the weights)

name: Describe the setting in which neural networks are related to computability: the type of network, the activation function, the encoding of words into numbers, and the definition of a network recognising a language.
answer:
Networks considered: recurrent networks (i.e. containing cycles)
• with real weights (in general);
• with one input neuron and one output neuron – the network computes a function F : A → ℝ, where A ⊆ ℝ contains all inputs on which the network stops;
• with the parallel activity rule: output values of all neurons are recomputed in every step;
• with the (saturated linear) activation function σ(ξ) = 1 for ξ ≥ 1; σ(ξ) = ξ for 0 ≤ ξ ≤ 1; σ(ξ) = 0 for ξ < 0.

Encoding of words: a word ω ∈ {0,1}+ is encoded into the number
δ(ω) = Σi=1..|ω| ω(i)/2i + 1/2|ω|+1.
E.g. ω = 11001 gives δ(ω) = 1/2 + 1/22 + 1/25 + 1/26 (= 0.110011 in binary form). The word is written as binary digits after the point and a final 1 is appended as an end marker, so that words differing e.g. in trailing zeros get different codes.

Recognising a language: a network recognises a language L ⊆ {0,1}+ if it computes a function F : A → ℝ (A ⊆ ℝ) such that
ω ∈ L iff δ(ω) ∈ A and F(δ(ω)) > 0.
That is, the network must stop on the code of every word of L and give a positive output on it.
keyPoints: Recurrent networks, real weights in general, one input and one output neuron
Parallel activity rule: all neurons recomputed in every step
Activation: 1 for ξ ≥ 1, ξ for 0 ≤ ξ ≤ 1, 0 for ξ < 0
Recognises L: ω ∈ L iff δ(ω) ∈ A and F(δ(ω)) > 0
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slides 51–52 (the end-marker remark explains the formula)

name: Which computability results hold for recurrent neural networks with rational and with real weights? (Exact neuron counts need not be memorised, but know the claims.)
answer:
Rational weights – Turing equivalence (Siegelmann & Sontag 1995): recurrent networks with rational weights are equivalent to Turing machines.
• For every recursively enumerable language L ⊆ {0,1}+ there is a recurrent network with rational weights and less than 1000 neurons which recognises L.
• The halting problem is undecidable already for networks with 25 neurons and rational weights.
• There is a "universal" network (an equivalent of the universal Turing machine).

Real weights – super-Turing power (Siegelmann & Sontag 1994): recurrent networks with real weights are super-Turing powerful.
• For every language L ⊆ {0,1}+ there is a recurrent network with less than 1000 neurons which recognises L (including languages that no Turing machine recognises).

Caveat (summary slide): the computability results need unbounded precision – a whole Turing machine tape is stored in the digits of one neuron's value – whereas real hardware computes with 4–32 bits.
keyPoints: Rational weights: equivalent to Turing machines
Every recursively enumerable language recognised by a small rational-weight network
Halting problem undecidable already for small networks; a universal network exists
Real weights: super-Turing – every language over {0,1} is recognised
Results need unbounded precision (the tape is stored in digits of a neuron's value)

name: Summarise the theoretical results on the expressive power of neural networks, explain why they are "purely theoretical", and compare neural networks with classical computers.
answer:
Neural networks are very strong from the point of view of theory:
• all Boolean functions can be expressed using two-layer networks;
• two-layer networks may approximate any continuous function (on a bounded closed domain);
• recurrent networks are at least as strong as Turing machines.

These results are purely theoretical:
• "theoretical" networks are extremely huge;
• it is very difficult to handcraft them even for the simplest problems;
• the computability results need unbounded precision (a whole Turing machine tape is stored in the digits of one neuron's value), while real hardware computes with 4–32 bits.
From the practical point of view, the most important advantages of neural networks are learning, generalization and robustness.

Neural networks vs. "classical" computers:
              Neural networks                  "Classical" computers
Data          implicitly in weights            explicitly
Computation   naturally parallel               sequential, localized
Robustness    robust w.r.t. input corruption   changing one bit may completely
              and damage                       crash the computation
Precision     approximate; similar inputs      (typically) precise
              give similar outputs
Programming   learning                         manual
keyPoints: Boolean functions: two-layer networks suffice
Continuous functions on a bounded closed domain: approximated by two-layer networks
Recurrent networks at least as strong as Turing machines
Purely theoretical: huge networks, hard to handcraft, unbounded precision
Practical advantages: learning, generalization, robustness
NN: data in weights, parallel, robust, approximate, learned; classical: explicit, sequential, fragile, precise, programmed
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slides 53–54 (slide 54 is a table)

name: Outline the history of neurocomputers and neural networks as presented in the lecture, from SNARC to the current boom.
answer:
Early neurocomputers:
• 1951 SNARC (Minsky et al.) – the first hardware implementation of a neural network; a simulated rat learns to find its way out of a maze; 40 artificial neurons (300 vacuum tubes, motors, etc.).
• 1957–60 Perceptron (Rosenblatt et al.) – the first successful network for image recognition; proposed 1957, simulated on an IBM 704 in 1958, the Mark I Perceptron hardware demonstrated in 1960. Only one layer of trainable weights (the intermediate "association" units were wired to the photocells randomly and never changed); image from 20 × 20 photocells; pixel intensities were inputs to a perceptron (basically the formal neuron); weights implemented by potentiometers, each set by its own motor; inputs could be arbitrarily reconnected to demonstrate adaptability.
• 1960 ADALINE (Widrow & Hoff) – a single-layer network; weights stored in the newly invented memistor, which remembers the history of electric current in the form of resistance. Widrow founded the Memistor Corporation; 1960–66 several neural-network companies were founded.

First AI winter:
• 1969 Minsky & Papert, Perceptrons – limits of single-layer perceptrons (e.g. XOR).
• ca. 1970–82 funding dries up, yet key ideas appear: SGD for multilayer networks (Amari 1967), reverse-mode automatic differentiation (Linnainmaa 1970), backpropagation for neural networks (Werbos 1974), Neocognitron – a pre-convolutional net (Fukushima 1980), Hopfield nets and Kohonen maps (1982).

Revival (1982 – end of the 90s): 1986 backpropagation popularised (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams); many attempts at hardware implementations (ASIC, FPGA), typically not better than software on universal computers (problems with weight storage, size, speed, production cost).

End of the 90s – ca. 2005: neural networks suppressed by other ML methods (support vector machines).

2006 – now: the boom. 2006 deep belief networks (Hinton et al.) – deep networks can be trained; 2012 AlexNet wins ImageNet on two GPUs – the start of the deep learning era; 2017 transformers; 2020s large language models; GPU implementations and specialised hardware (Google's TPU); 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics to Hopfield and Hinton, in Chemistry to Hassabis and Jumper (AlphaFold) and Baker.
keyPoints: 1951 SNARC – first hardware neural network; 1957–60 Rosenblatt's Perceptron; 1960 ADALINE with memistors
1969 Minsky & Papert show limits of single-layer perceptrons (XOR) → first AI winter
Key ideas still appear during the winter (SGD, reverse-mode autodiff, backpropagation, Neocognitron, Hopfield)
1986 backpropagation popularised; revival; hardware attempts not better than software
Late 90s–2005: suppressed by SVMs
2006 deep belief nets, 2012 AlexNet, 2017 transformers, 2020s LLMs

name: What does the lecture say about the scale of current deep learning (data and model sizes), what we got in return, and why benchmarks are called "a treadmill"? Include the caveats about benchmark results.
answer:
Highlights: breakthroughs in image recognition, game playing (superhuman Go, chess, poker; grandmaster level in StarCraft II), machine translation and speech processing, science (AlphaFold; gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad), and text/multimodal generation (large language models, coding agents, image and video generation).

Scale – what do we face:
• Increasing dataset size: weakly-supervised pre-training on 3.6 × 109 Instagram images; LLMs are pre-trained on 1.5–3.6 × 1013 tokens of text; GPT-3 used 45 TB of compressed text filtered to approx. 570 GB.
• …and thus increasing size of networks: from ADALINE through early backpropagation networks, LeNet-5, deep belief networks (where the third "wave" started), GPU-accelerated MLPs and AlexNet to GoogLeNet. The sizes of the largest commercial models are not disclosed; a 2023 leak claimed ≈ 1.8 × 1012 parameters for GPT-4 as a mixture of experts (only a fraction of the weights is used for each token); disclosed open-weight models have hundreds of billions to a trillion parameters with only tens of billions active per token.

What did we get: since deep networks reached the necessary scale they have won the ImageNet challenge every year with lower and lower error rates, and benchmark after benchmark in vision, speech, language understanding and mathematical reasoning has been conquered.

Benchmarks – a treadmill: every benchmark starts with low frontier scores and becomes saturated (MNIST, ImageNet, MMLU, MATH, GPQA Diamond, …), after which a harder successor is introduced (SWE-bench Verified → SWE-bench Pro, ARC-AGI-2 → ARC-AGI-3). The time from "frontier < 10 %" to "> 80 %" shrank from years (ImageNet, MMLU) to months (FrontierMath, ARC-AGI-2). The newest evaluations measure agents, not answers: long-horizon coding, real economic tasks, tool use – and cost per task.

Caveats: mostly self-reported scores; results with vs. without tools differ; contamination; label errors; and a saturated benchmark says nothing about which model is better.
keyPoints: Datasets: billions of images, 10^13 tokens of text
Model sizes grew to ~10^12 parameters; mixture of experts uses only a fraction per token
Reward: steadily falling error rates across vision, speech, language, math benchmarks
Treadmill: benchmarks saturate and are replaced; years → months
Newest evaluations measure agents and cost per task
Caveats: self-reported, tools vs. no tools, contamination, label errors, saturation is uninformative
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slides 61–68 (slides 64, 66, 67 are charts; slide 68 is a table)

name: What matters in AI hardware? Contrast CPU and GPU/TPU, list the five parameters with the question each one answers, and say what limits training and what limits inference. What do the server/rack examples and the six-year table show?
answer:
CPU vs. GPU/TPU: a CPU has a few powerful cores for branching, sequential code; a GPU/TPU has thousands of simple units that multiply matrices – and a layer of a neural network is essentially one matrix multiplication.

Five parameters and their questions:
1. Compute (FLOPS) and number format – how many multiply-adds per second? FP32 → BF16 → FP8 → FP4: every halving of bits roughly doubles throughput.
2. Memory capacity (HBM per GPU) – does the model fit?
3. Memory bandwidth – how fast can the weights be read?
4. Interconnect – how fast do GPUs talk to each other? Scale-up inside a rack (NVLink) vs. much slower scale-out between racks (InfiniBand/Ethernet).
5. Power – today the real limit (kW per rack, GW per cluster).

Training is mostly limited by compute and interconnect; inference (text generation) by memory.

Examples: a 2020 DGX A100 server has 8 GPUs with 80 GB HBM each, is air cooled (6.5 kW) and fits in a normal rack; a 2024 GB200 NVL72 rack has 72 GPUs with 192 GB each in one NVLink domain – the rack behaves like one giant GPU – needs about 120 kW and liquid cooling. In the DGX A100 the two CPUs are there to feed the GPUs with data; in the GB200 rack 36 Grace CPUs are paired with the GPUs. (Historically: in 2012 Google trained a 1-billion-connection network on 1000 computers with 16 000 cores for three days; in 2013 the same scale was reached on 3 GPU servers.)

Lessons of the six-year table (A100 → Rubin):
• compute per GPU grew far more (≈160×) than memory bandwidth (≈11×) – the "memory wall": moving data, not arithmetic, is the bottleneck;
• most of the compute gain comes from lower precision (FP16 → FP8 → FP4) and from scale-up (72 GPUs act as one), not from faster cores;
• consequence: numerics (FP8/FP4 training and inference) is now a first-class topic in deep learning.
keyPoints: GPU/TPU = thousands of simple units multiplying matrices; a layer ≈ one matrix multiplication
Compute and number format; memory capacity; memory bandwidth; interconnect; power
Halving the bits roughly doubles throughput
Training limited by compute and interconnect, inference by memory
Memory wall: compute grew much faster than memory bandwidth
Gains come from lower precision and scale-up, not faster cores
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slides 69–72 and 74 (slide 74 is a table)

name: Practical: Use the lecture's two rules of thumb. For a model with 70 billion parameters, estimate (a) the memory needed for inference in FP16 and in FP4, (b) the memory needed for training, and (c) at most how many text pieces per second one GPU with 8 TB/s memory bandwidth can generate for the FP4 model. Explain the reasoning behind each rule.
answer:
Rule 1 – Does it fit? A model with P parameters needs
• for inference: P × (bytes per parameter);
• for training: ≈ 16 bytes per parameter (weights, gradients and the optimizer's bookkeeping) plus memory for the intermediate results of the forward pass.

(a) Inference, P = 70 × 109:
• FP16 = 2 bytes per parameter → 70 × 109 × 2 = 140 GB, i.e. two A100 GPUs (80 GB each);
• FP4 = 0.5 byte per parameter → 35 GB, which fits on one GPU.

(b) Training: 70 × 109 × 16 bytes ≈ 1.1 TB for the parameters alone, i.e. at least 6 Blackwell GPUs (192 GB each) – plus the forward-pass intermediate results.

Rule 2 – How fast does it write? A language model writes text piece by piece (tokens, roughly word fragments); for every piece, all weights must be read from memory once. Hence
pieces/s ≤ memory bandwidth / model size in bytes (an upper bound).

(c) 8 TB/s ÷ 35 GB ≈ 230 pieces/s at most.

Consequence: the arithmetic units mostly wait for data. Answering many users at once (each weight is read once and used for all of them) is what makes inference efficient. This is also why inference is limited by memory (capacity and bandwidth) rather than by compute.
keyPoints: Inference memory = P × bytes per parameter: 140 GB in FP16, 35 GB in FP4
Training ≈ 16 bytes per parameter (weights, gradients, optimizer state) + forward-pass intermediates ≈ 1.1 TB
Each generated piece requires reading all weights once
pieces/s ≤ memory bandwidth / model size: at most 8 TB/s ÷ 35 GB ≈ 230
Batching many users reuses each weight read – that makes it efficient
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slide 73 (GPU capacities from slides 71–72)

name: Give the advantages and disadvantages of doing deep learning in clouds, and characterise the current software frameworks (PyTorch, JAX, Keras 3, TensorFlow and the historical ones).
answer:
Deep learning in clouds. Big companies offer cloud services (Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure), there are GPU clouds (CoreWeave, Lambda, …) and academic infrastructure that is free for students (MetaCentrum / e-INFRA CZ, IT4Innovations, EuroHPC supercomputers).
Advantages: you do not have to care (too much) about technical problems; you do not have to buy and optimize high-end hardware/software, networks etc.; scaling and virtually limitless storage.
Disadvantages: you do not have full control; performance can vary and there may be connectivity problems; you have to pay for the services; privacy issues.

Current software.
• PyTorch (Meta / PyTorch Foundation) – the de facto standard: the vast majority of research code and most open-weight models; eager (define-by-run) execution, object-oriented API, torch.compile for graph-level optimization; ecosystem: Hugging Face transformers, PyTorch Lightning, vLLM (inference).
• JAX (Google) – NumPy-like functional API plus composable transformations (grad, jit, vmap); built for TPUs and large-scale distributed training; Flax and Optax are built on top.
• Keras 3 – a high-level model API, now backend-agnostic (runs on PyTorch, JAX or TensorFlow); good for teaching and quick prototyping of standard architectures.
• TensorFlow (Google) – dominant 2016–2019, now mostly in maintenance mode; still common in production/mobile.
• Historical: Theano (the grand-daddy of them all, strongly inspired TensorFlow), Caffe, Torch (Lua), Chainer – all discontinued.
keyPoints: Cloud pros: no hardware/technical worries, scaling, virtually limitless storage
Cloud cons: no full control, variable performance/connectivity, cost, privacy
PyTorch: de facto standard, eager define-by-run, object-oriented
JAX: functional NumPy-like API with grad/jit/vmap; Flax and Optax on top
Keras 3: high-level, backend-agnostic; TensorFlow: mostly maintenance mode
Theano, Caffe, Torch (Lua), Chainer are discontinued
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slides 75–76 and 80

name: Practical (code): The lecture implements the same multilayer perceptron for XOR in JAX, Flax (NNX) and PyTorch. Describe the model and the training procedure the code implements, and explain how the three versions differ in the way gradients and weight updates are expressed.
answer:
What all three programs do:
• Data: the four XOR inputs X = [[0,0],[0,1],[1,0],[1,1]] with targets y = [[0],[1],[1],[0]].
• Model: an MLP 2 → 8 → 1: a hidden layer of 8 neurons with ReLU and a linear output layer.
• Initialization: He initialization of the weights (normal samples scaled by √(2/m), m = number of inputs of the layer), zero biases – explicit in the JAX and PyTorch versions; the Flax version uses the default random initialization of nnx.Linear.
• Loss: mean squared error, mean((model(X) − y)2).
• Training: 2000 steps of gradient descent on the whole dataset with learning rate 0.1, w ← w − lr · grad.
• Result: the rounded outputs are [[0],[1],[1],[0]], i.e. the network has learned XOR.

JAX (functional): parameters are an explicit list of (W, b) pairs; mlp(params, x) and loss(params, X, y) are pure functions. jax.grad(loss) returns a function computing the gradients by automatic differentiation; the update is written by hand with jax.tree.map(lambda p, g: p - lr * g, params, grads) and returns new parameters; @jax.jit compiles the step.

Flax (NNX): the model is a class (nnx.Module) with nnx.Linear layers; the optimizer comes from Optax (optax.sgd(0.1)) wrapped in nnx.Optimizer. nnx.grad(loss)(model) differentiates with respect to the model, and opt.update(model, grads) performs w ← w − lr · grad.

PyTorch (object-oriented, eager): nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 8), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(8, 1)), nn.MSELoss(), torch.optim.SGD. Each iteration calls opt.zero_grad() (clear old gradients), computes the loss, loss.backward() (gradients by autodiff, stored in the parameters) and opt.step() (in-place update).

In all cases the gradient is obtained by automatic differentiation (backpropagation) – the programmer writes only the forward computation and the loss.
keyPoints: MLP 2-8-1, ReLU hidden layer, linear output, trained on the four XOR examples
He initialization (scale √(2/m)), zero biases
Mean squared error; 2000 gradient-descent steps with learning rate 0.1
JAX: pure functions, jax.grad, manual update via tree.map, jit
Flax: nnx.Module + Optax optimizer, nnx.grad and opt.update
PyTorch: zero_grad → loss.backward() → opt.step() on stateful objects
